title: The Labour Day Gap: What a Public Holiday in One State Quietly Costs a Multi-State Business
linkedin:
New South Wales stood still today for Labour Day. Queensland and Victoria did not.

If your business only trades in one state, that's a trivia fact. If it trades across state lines, it's a cash flow timing problem most forecasts never catch.

Here's the pattern. A Sydney site either loses a full trading day or pays public holiday penalty rates on every hour worked, cutting into margin on exactly the hours it's open. A Brisbane or Melbourne site, meanwhile, trades through an entirely ordinary Monday. Same business, same month, two different weeks.

It gets quieter still. Banks and payment networks follow the public holiday calendar of the state they're processing in, not the state the invoice was raised in. A payment initiated from a Sydney account today can sit until tomorrow before it clears, while a Brisbane counterpart's bank runs its usual overnight cycle. On its own, a one day lag is nothing. Stacked against a week that already has a debtor chasing up and a wage run due, it's exactly the kind of gap that turns a tight week into a short one.

Most 13-week cash flow forecasts spread revenue and costs evenly across every week, because that's the simplest model to build. It's also the model most likely to miss the handful of weeks each year that aren't actually ordinary. Queensland has its own Labour Day in May. Victoria has Melbourne Cup Day in November. Each one quietly repeats the same mismatch.

The fix isn't complicated. Map the full public holiday calendar for every state you trade in, once, and mark it against the weeks it touches.

A note for business owners trading across more than one state this Australian Small Business Month.

New South Wales, the ACT and South Australia marked Labour Day today, the first Monday in October. Queensland already had its own Labour Day back in May, and Victoria does not observe the day at all. For a business trading only inside one state, that is a minor calendar detail. For a business with a site, a client base or even a few staff on the other side of a state border, it is a cash flow timing gap that is easy to miss and tends to repeat several times a year.

The pattern shows up in a few places. A site in the state observing the holiday either loses a trading day or pays public holiday penalty rates on every hour it stays open. A site in a state not observing it trades through an ordinary Monday. Bank payments can also run a day behind when they are processed from an account in the state taking the holiday.

None of this needs to be a surprise. Mapping each state's public holiday calendar against the cash flow forecast once, rather than noticing the gap after it has already landed, keeps the numbers honest all year.
